title: Integral closure of a one-dimensional Noetherian domain in a finite extension
statement: Let A be a Noetherian domain of Krull dimension 1 [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring] with fraction field K, let L be a finite field extension of K, and let C be the integral closure of A in L [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure]. Then C is a Dedekind domain (a Noetherian integrally closed domain of Krull dimension 1 [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]), and the map $\operatorname{Spec}(C) \to \operatorname{Spec}(A)$ is surjective with finite fibres and induces finite residue field extensions.

proof.text: Let D=C be the integral closure of A in L. Since A ⊆ C ⊆ L, the Krull–Akizuki theorem [lem-sc-krull-akizuki-noetherian] shows that C is Noetherian.

source.place: Algebra Lemma 09IG, first sentence, invoking Lemma 10.119.12 (Tag 00PG)

proof.text: The inclusion A → C is integral and injective, and C is a subring of the field L. Therefore the integral-extension dimension equality [lem-weil-pbc-integral-injective-dimension-equal] gives dim(C)=dim(A)=1. The integral closure C is integrally closed in L and is a domain, and its fraction field is L, by [lem-weil-pbc-integral-closure-finite-extension-normal]. Hence C is a Noetherian integrally closed domain of dimension 1, i.e. a Dedekind domain.

source.place: Algebra Lemma 09IG, second and third sentences, invoking Lemmas 10.112.4 (Tag 00OK) and 10.120.17 (Tag 034X)

proof.text: The inclusion A ⊆ C is integral, so lying over [lem-weil-pbc-integral-injective-lying-over] says that every prime of A is the contraction of a prime of C. Thus Spec(C) → Spec(A) is surjective.

source.place: Algebra Lemma 09IG, fourth sentence, invoking Lemma 10.36.17 (Tag 00GQ)

proof.text: For every maximal ideal m of A, localize A at A\m and C at the same multiplicative set. By the localization prime correspondence [lem-weil-pbc-localization-prime-residue-field-iso] (1), applied to C → (A\m)⁻¹C with W = A\m, contraction is a bijection from the primes of (A\m)⁻¹C onto the primes of C disjoint from A\m; since A is one-dimensional, a prime of C is disjoint from A\m exactly when it contracts to (0) or to m, and the primes lying over mA_m correspond exactly to the primes of C over m. By part (3) of the same statement, corresponding primes have isomorphic residue fields as C-algebras, hence as A-algebras. The resulting injective map A_m → (A\m)⁻¹C is between domains, its fraction fields are K and L, and A_m is Noetherian local of dimension 1. Thus [lem-weil-pbc-dim-one-residue-field-extensions-finite] gives finitely many primes over m, each maximal, and finite residue-field extensions. For the generic prime (0), any prime q of C contracting to (0) contains (0), and incomparability for the integral extension A ⊆ C forces q=(0), so the generic fibre has one point; its residue extension is Frac(C)=L over Frac(A)=K, finite by hypothesis. Hence every fibre is finite, and all residue-field extensions are finite.

source.place: Algebra Lemma 09IG, final sentence, invoking Lemma 10.119.10 (Tag 031F)
